title: English river trout density was lower below storm overflows with more spill hours, but heavy rain, spring rain and warm spells before surveys added no overflow-specific loss (1995-2024)
abstract: Question: do storm overflows lower salmonid fish density in English rivers, and do heavy rain, a wet spring or a warm spell add a loss below overflows? Data: Environment Agency electric-fishing surveys (first-run density, 1995-2024), 15,273 overflow outlet points from EDM returns 2021-2025 routed on OS Open Rivers, E-OBS daily rain and temperature. Outlets 0-5 km upstream are the exposure; outlets 0-5 km downstream are a placebo. A plan was written before the fish models. Results: (1) No planned weather test met the support rule. In 24,118 July-October surveys at 4,716 sites, heavy-rain days in the 28 days before the survey x upstream outlets gave +0.0020 log density per day per doubling of outlets (95% CI -0.0041 to +0.0081); spring rain gave -0.0001 (SE 0.0015); a warm 28 days gave -0.0081 per C (SE 0.0037, Holm p 0.085) but -0.0048 near downstream outlets, so the overflow-specific contrast was -0.0034 (SE 0.0057). Rain lowered catches at all sites (-0.026 per day). The CI excludes losses above 0.1 within-site SD. (2) Within-site spill-year changes (2021-2025) gave no loss (+0.002, SE 0.019). (3) Between sites, salmonid density fell by 0.056 per log(1 + upstream spill hours) against 0.011 for downstream hours (difference -0.045, SE 0.010), the same in 1995-2009; the deficit came from trout, not salmon, and tolerant cyprinids were denser below outlets. (4) Post hoc, at 1,701 outlets with sites above and below, the below-minus-above difference decreased by 0.033 (SE 0.012) per log spill hour, with or without river-size and town-size controls and at network overflows without treatment works. The average level contrast changed sign with river-size controls, so we do not claim it. Conclusion: a chronic deficit that grows with overflow use, not a pulse after storms. Limitations: associations only; outlet map 2021-2025 applied to earlier years; no flow or water-quality data; air temperature, not water temperature; England only.
